why.say:
Okay, quick game. It's called Better Question. I've got two questions up on the board, and you vote with your hands.

Question one: “Was it because you had no car?” Question two: “What, if anything, made it hard to get seen sooner?” Hands up for one. Now hands up for two.

{name}, I see you, you went with one. You've got ten seconds to defend it. Go.

Here's the reveal. Question one gets you a yes. Question two gets you the truth.

The only gap explanation that survives an adjuster is John Doe's own, in his own words, backed by paper you can check: a work schedule, a doctor's availability note, a receipt.

So your job is to draw it out and write it down exactly as he says it. You don't explain it for him. You don't defend it, and you definitely don't judge it.

One more thing before we move on. By the end of this block, I'm going to show you how one friendly little sentence on this call can hand the defense their whole argument.

Remember it this way: you're the stenographer, not the defense lawyer.
why.ask: {name}, which of those two questions would the defense lawyer rather you asked John Doe, and why?

theory.say:
So here's the road for the gap interview, nice and simple. You plan your questions, never the answers you're hoping for.

You open on the record with the date, your role and his consent to record. Then you ask open questions and follow his words. You ask for the paper, you read his story back to him, and you write it all down, with a dated task for every document he mentions.

Underneath all of it sits one rule: coordinate, don't commingle. That just means the medical side and the legal side don't get mixed up in your notes.

You write facts, never conclusions. Why? Because your opinion in a note is something the defense gets to use.

Honestly, TV has ruined us a little. On TV the detective pounds the table and the witness cracks.

On this job, the detective asks a soft open question, then shuts up and types. {name}, which of those two do you think actually gets the truth?

The one thing to keep: ask soft, then shut up and type.
theory.ask: {name}, why is staying quiet after an open question so much harder than it sounds?

frame.say:
Let's bring back A-C-T, because the gap interview lives right inside it. A-C-T is our three-step plan the minute something goes wrong in care: Assess, Coordinate, Track.

Before I walk through it, {name}, take a guess. Is a gap in treatment a medical danger or a legal danger? Hold that thought.

Assess comes first. A medical danger, like a fever or a screw coming loose after surgery, goes to the doctor today. A legal danger, like a gap or a vague note, goes to Atty. Thorne.

And there's your answer: a gap is a legal danger.

Then Coordinate. You call the provider's office to clarify, and you clear whatever barrier the client names, whether that's rides, scheduling or a referral.

Track means you write down the flag and every fix you tried, that same day. Then it's back to monitoring, and the question is always the same: is the plan working?

Anybody can flag it and forget it. The Case Manager we want flags it, knocks down the barrier, and checks back in.

A-C-T in one line: spot it, fix it, write it down.
frame.ask: {name}, looking at John Doe's file right now, which step of A-C-T is his 14-Day Gap sitting in?

rules.say:
Okay, the rules for the gap call. You investigate; you don't advocate.

Read the EMS report, the 02/20/2026 urgent-care history and the timeline, then write a plan that holds questions only. Nothing else.

Run it like a funnel. Broad open questions first, then follow-ups built on his words, and short yes-or-no questions last, only to pin down a date or a document. Never lead, and never judge.

You already know the usual reasons, like rides, co-pays and work schedules. You just never offer them to him.

Record only with his spoken consent. If Keystone wants a Recorded Statement, which is the insurance company taping his version of events, he politely declines and sends them to us.

Confirm his 03/05/2026 consult with Dr. Reyes, and ask how he'll get to care once the rental ends 03/19/2026.

Now, that friendly sentence I promised you: “Don't worry, the gap won't matter.” Sounds kind, right? It's legal advice. Reassure the process, never the outcome.

And when a client says “I was busy,” that's not an explanation, that's a chapter title. {name}, what's your next question? Right: “Busy with what?”
rules.ask: {name}, if John Doe's reason is true anyway, why does it matter how you asked for it?

model.say:
Have a look at this board. Before I explain anything, {name}, read me the first green line and the first red line out loud. Thank you.

On the left, in green, it says ask it open. On the right, in red, never like this. Every open question sits on the same line as the leading version it replaces, so you can read straight across and actually hear the difference.

See that last red row with the little UPL tag? UPL is the unauthorized practice of law, which is giving legal advice when you're not a lawyer.

That row is the soothing line. Kind on the surface, an opinion on his case underneath.

Down below is the funnel: open first, then follow his words, then pin the dates and documents. And notice the pill at its mouth: recorded, consent on the record.

Here's the thing. Same fact, asked two ways, gives you two different cases. The rushed call fires off the red column. The good call asks the green column, slowly.
model.ask: {name}, reading across the rows, which red question do you think you'd be most tempted to ask on a real call?

job.say:
Now let's follow this on the job. It starts when the records show the 14-day gap.

You read the EMS report, the urgent-care history and the treatment timeline in the CMS. Then you save your question plan in Case Notes before the call, with no question in it naming a reason.

When the call connects in the Call Simulator with AI John Doe, you state the date, who's on, and that it's recorded. You get his consent and confirm he's somewhere private.

True story, more or less: I once had a client take this call from a packed barbershop, with three guys chiming in on what really happened. Privilege, which keeps our talk with the client protected, does not love an audience.

If he asks what the gap does to his case, no opinion. Log it and send it to Atty. Thorne through Tasks the same day.

So why all this care? Because months from now the adjuster will read that gap and try to knock thousands off the offer. A clean, documented explanation is what keeps that money on the table.

No opinions on the call, just his words, logged and routed.
job.ask: {name}, where in that sequence do you think a nervous new Case Manager is most likely to slip?

dodont.say:
Time for 3 Clues, 1 Rule. I'll reveal three clues one at a time. As soon as you think you've got it, call Do or Don't and name the rule behind it. Right call, one point.

{name}, you're keeping score. {name}, you're up first.

The good habits: asking open, following his words and closing last. Reading his story back so he can correct you. And preventing the next gap now, which is way cheaper than explaining a second one in the demand.

The traps: a question that names the reason you expect, blaming him for the gap, and soothing. Honestly, “Don't worry” is the most common UPL slip in this whole module.

Now, a mystery to carry into the next lesson. The adjuster is going to say this gap proves John Doe healed.

Somewhere on his file is a piece of paper, made before anyone was thinking about a claim, that says otherwise. {name}, find it before I show it.
dodont.ask: {name}, what's the difference between telling John consistent care matters and telling him what this gap does to his case?

why.say:
Hands up if you've ever ghosted someone. Come on, a friend, a dentist, a gym that kept calling. Keep them up. Now keep them up if you felt a little guilty about it. Yep.

Clients ghost us too, and almost never because they're bad people. They're in pain, they're overwhelmed, they changed phones.

And when you finally do get a text back, it says “new phone, who dis.” That's not a client, that's a plot twist.

So here's my teaser. This lesson isn't really about chasing a client. It's about something sneakier: when a client goes quiet, the case keeps running without them. The deadlines don't stop.

The No Contact Protocol, which is just our step-by-step plan for when a client stops answering, does three jobs. It tracks the silence officially, it proves the firm tried hard before anyone talks about ending the case, and it protects the firm if somebody later asks, what did you do?

{name}, I'll tell you which of those three matters most in a minute. Make your guess now.

Here's the line to keep: silence stops the client, never the clock.
why.ask: {name}, if John Doe went quiet tomorrow, who gets hurt if nobody can prove what the firm did to reach him?

theory.say:
Here's the road, nice and plain. First you look inside the file before you call anyone: the case status, the deadlines, the last time we spoke.

Then you reach out, and you climb a ladder. Two phone calls, then email and text, then the emergency contact, then a certified letter, which is mail where the post office gives us proof it was delivered. After that, you tell Atty. Thorne what the silence puts at risk.

A few words you'll hear. Due diligence just means proof we made a real, reasonable effort, written down. Approved channels are the ways the client agreed at intake we could contact them, and only those count.

And the emergency contact is the backup person who can still reach the client. So, guess who that is on John Doe's file. {name}?

It's Margaret Doe, his mother. Remember that name, okay? She gets very important in about ten minutes.

Look inside first, then climb the ladder, then tell Atty. Thorne.
theory.ask: {name}, where on John Doe's file would you look to find his approved contact channels?

frame.say:
Before I show you this list, {name}, a quick bet. Do clients go silent out of nowhere, or is there usually a warning sign? Hold that.

Here's the reveal: silence almost always starts with a bottleneck, which is just a spot where the work slows down or gets stuck.

Missing information, like a wrong phone number or no incident details. Slow follow-up, where we asked a question and nobody chased the answer. A Conflict Check, the search to make sure we don't already represent the other side, stuck in a backlog.

Then there are intake forms with wrong dates or missing signatures, facts so unclear the attorney has to review them, and plain old communication gaps between departments.

A weak Case Manager says, “the client went dark.” A great one asks, “what did we do that made it easy for them to drift?”

And it matters, because every one of these bottlenecks weakens the eventual demand. A gap on our side looks like a gap in the case.

Remember: before you blame the client, check our own bottlenecks.
frame.ask: {name}, looking at John Doe's file right now, which of these bottlenecks do you think he's closest to?

rules.say:
Okay, the rules, and the one habit that separates the pros. Step 1 is internal review: check the status, the live deadlines and the last contact date before you dial. Everybody wants to skip it. Don't.

Step 2 is the ladder: at least two phone calls, then email and text, then the emergency contact, then certified mail or a formal letter.

And this is where people fail. You climb by channel, not by volume.

Calling the same cell number nine times and writing “tried everything” isn't trying everything. Bonus points if his voicemail box was full the whole time, so you basically left nine messages for a robot that says the mailbox is full.

What good looks like is two calls, then an email, then a text, then Margaret. Each one logged with date, time, channel and outcome, and a follow-up reminder set.

Step 3 is telling Atty. Thorne, because deadlines don't pause for silence.

And the line you don't cross, {name}: you can tell the client what we need and by when. You can't tell them we're dropping their case.

Burn it in: climb by channel, not by volume.
rules.ask: {name}, before you pick up the phone, what deadline is already running on John Doe's file?

model.say:
Here's the whole protocol in one picture, and there's a little hidden lesson in how it's drawn.

Down the left is a spine of six stations. The first three are in full colour: internal review, contact attempts and team notification. That's today. Stations four to six are greyed out with a next lesson tag.

On the right, station two opens into a ladder of channels: phone, then email and text, then the emergency contact, then certified mail.

Now look closely. {name}, what do you notice about the size of the rungs? Yep, each one gets wider.

That's the hidden lesson. Every step up reaches further and costs more effort, so you don't skip rungs, and you don't stand on one rung forever either.

And down in the corner, the red card. The statute of limitations, which is the legal deadline to file the lawsuit, keeps running the whole time.

Every rung reaches further. Use each one, then step up.
model.ask: {name}, why do you think each rung on that ladder is drawn wider than the one above it?

job.say:
Let me tell you how this plays out for real. A Case Manager I trained once logged eleven calls to a silent client in two days. Eleven. She was so proud.

Turns out the client had dropped his phone in a lake while fishing. Every one of those calls went straight to the bottom of the lake. One email would've reached him in an hour.

So here's the job. John Doe misses an appointment. That's your trigger. You open the Case Summary in the CMS and do Step 1, so you know the live deadlines.

Then you work the ladder in the Communications Log, the file's diary of every contact, logging each attempt with date, time, channel and outcome.

When the ladder's done, you escalate to Atty. Thorne through Tasks, with the impact spelled out: the SOL of 02/06/2028 and any hearing dates.

Why bother? Because an adjuster who sees a client vanish assumes the injuries weren't that bad. {name}, our log is how we prove otherwise.
job.ask: {name}, what would Atty. Thorne need to see in that escalation before acting on it?

dodont.say:
Game time: 3 Clues, 1 Rule. I reveal one clue at a time. The moment you know where it's going, shout Do or Don't and name the rule. Get it right three times and you win bragging rights for the day.

{name}, you're on the buzzer first.

Some rounds are good habits, like setting a follow-up reminder the second a request goes out, or giving the client an easy way to answer: a call window, a text, an upload link.

Some are traps, like letting a file sit with nothing logged because “we're waiting on the client,” or blaming the client for what's really our own process gap.

And listen hard for channel versus volume. Honestly, it's the one people miss most.

Now, your mystery for the next activity. John Doe's file shows two calls to his mobile on the phone system and zero entries in the log. {name}, figure out what that missing log costs us.
dodont.ask: {name}, why does calling Margaret count as a new channel when a third call to John's mobile doesn't?

why.say:
Quick game. Would you rather spend five hundred dollars hiring someone to find a missing person, or spend five dollars on a letter that might make them call you back?

Hands up for the letter. Everybody? Good. Then you already get this lesson.

The Final Warning Letter is the last cheap step before the firm has to pick between two expensive ones: paying to find the client, or the attorney moving to end the case.

So the letter has two jobs. It has to be specific enough that the client actually answers, and documented enough to back up whatever comes next.

Now here's the teaser. There's one mistake that wastes the firm's money and weakens the whole record, and honestly, new Case Managers make it all the time. It's about three things being true at the same time.

{name}, I'll reveal it on the next slide. Take a guess at what the three things are.

The takeaway: the cheap letter always comes before the expensive search.
why.ask: {name}, what's the risk of spending the firm's money on a search before the letter's deadline has even passed?

theory.say:
Here's the reveal I promised. This letter is one last written notice before the firm searches for the client or the attorney moves to withdraw.

It goes two ways at once. Certified mail proves it was delivered. Email is what people actually read. Each one covers the other's blind spot.

Because certified mail has one secret talent: nobody is ever home to sign for it. That little green card comes back unclaimed more reliably than anything else in this business.

Then there's the three-criteria gate. Think of it like a door with three locks: the ladder is done, the letter is sent, and the letter's deadline has passed. All three, not one.

Only then do we skip-trace, which is just a paid search for someone's current address and phone number. It costs the firm money, so the attorney has to approve it.

And withdrawal, meaning the firm officially stops representing the client, is decided only by the attorney, under firm and court rules. {name}, which of those three locks do you think people forget to check?

Three locks, all open, or the door stays shut.
theory.ask: {name}, which of these terms have you met before, and where would it show up on John Doe's file?

frame.say:
Before I show you the next three steps, {name}, give me a prediction. Of Steps 4, 5 and 6, how many does the Case Manager actually drive? Hold your number.

Step 4 is the Final Warning Letter. It lists every earlier attempt, gives the client 7 to 14 days to respond, and warns that the firm may withdraw. It goes by certified mail and email.

Step 5 is the decision point. If there's still no answer, the attorney decides whether to file a Notice or a Motion to Withdraw, which is the paperwork telling the court the firm is stepping off the case.

Step 6 is closing the file, marked “No response, withdrew per protocol,” with every proof kept.

And the reveal: you really drive just one of them, the letter. But you build the record that makes the other two possible.

A sloppy letter turns Step 5 into a gamble. A clean one makes it routine.
frame.ask: {name}, if John Doe went silent today, how far would his file be from Step 4?

rules.say:
Okay, the rules. Step 4 goes by certified mail and email. Both, not either. The letter lists the earlier attempts, sets a deadline of 7 to 14 days and warns that withdrawal is possible.

And confirm the address first. I once saw a perfect warning letter, beautifully written, mailed to the client's old apartment.

The new tenant signed for it, read it, and called us asking if he could take over the case. True story, more or less. A letter to a stale address proves nothing.

At Step 5, the attorney may file to withdraw. That's counsel's call. Skip-tracing starts only when all three locks are open and counsel approves it with the full log attached.

“We've tried several times” tells a judge nothing. “Called 02/10, voicemail 02/13,” and so on, with real dates, tells them everything.

The letter can say withdrawal is possible. {name}, what it can never do is judge the claim or announce the case is over.
rules.ask: {name}, why both certified mail and email, when either one would technically get the letter there?

model.say:
Two panels here, and the most important thing on this slide is one tiny word. See if you can spot it.

On the left is the letter on letterhead, with four orange badges marking what it has to contain: the earlier attempts, listed; a response deadline of 7 to 14 days; notice that withdrawal is possible; and how to respond.

Above it, certified mail and email, joined by a bold AND. That's the tiny word, {name}. Not or. And.

On the right is the Step 5 fork. It starts with one question: did a response come in by the deadline? If yes, the file picks right back up.

If no, you hit a gate with three chips: ladder done, letter sent, deadline passed. Only then do you reach the skip-trace and the attorney's decision.

It's drawn as a gate on purpose, honestly, because people love to sneak around it.
model.ask: {name}, what happens on this picture if only two of those three chips are true?

job.say:
Here's how it runs on the job. Your Step 3 escalation is done and there's still nothing.

So you draft the Final Warning Letter in the Action Plan Editor, the screen where we build letters and plans from the firm's templates. Every earlier attempt listed, deadline and withdrawal notice in place.

You confirm the current address and send it from CMS Documents, Outgoing, by certified mail and email. Both logged, certified receipt kept.

Then the deadline passes. And of course, the day after, the client strolls back in with, “Hey, did you guys need something?” Like he just went out for milk.

That's fine, because the log still proves we did everything right. Now you check all three locks in the log, and only then do you escalate to Atty. Thorne through Tasks, asking for skip-trace approval and the Step 5 decision.

Why all this paperwork? Because if this case ever goes sideways, a judge or a bar complaint looks at exactly this record. A clean letter protects the client's claim, the firm and you.

{name}, which piece of this would you be most nervous about getting wrong?

Remember: the record you build today is the defense you'll need tomorrow.
job.ask: {name}, what's the first thing you'd check in the log before you escalate to Atty. Thorne?

dodont.say:
3 Clues, 1 Rule, round two. Three clues, one at a time. The second you've got it, call Do or Don't and name the rule. {name}, you're up first, and the rest of you can steal if they miss.

You'll see good habits, like listing attempts with real dates, because “we have tried several times” isn't evidence. Or asking in-house help to confirm an address you can't verify.

You'll see traps, like triggering a skip-trace when only one lock is open, or writing “we are withdrawing” in a letter the attorney never approved.

That's the hard line. You build the record; the attorney decides to withdraw.

On Day 5 we'll go deep on skip-tracing, on process servers, the people who hand court papers to someone in person, and on certified notice. Today's just the trigger.

Now your mystery for the drafting activity. Atty. Thorne wants a letter that's urgent but not threatening. {name}, find the one sentence in a typical draft that quietly turns urgent into a threat.
dodont.ask: {name}, who decides that representation is ending, and who tells the client?

case.say:
Something just landed on the file. Before I reveal it, {name}, guess how many days a client can go quiet before it's a problem. Shout a number.

Here it is, dated 02/16/2026, file LSH-2026-MVA-770412. Six days with no contact from John Doe. His last logged contact was 02/10/2026, and he missed his check-in call on 02/13/2026.

The phone system shows two calls to his mobile, both voicemail. And here's the twist: neither one is in the Communications Log, the file's diary of every contact.

No treatment start recorded. His emergency contact is Margaret Doe, at (555) 010-2291, and Step 1 of the No Contact Protocol is due today.

Check that number before you climb the ladder, by the way. I once called a client's number on file three times and got the same pizza place every time. By call three, they had my order memorized.

Now, {name}, read the bad log entry out loud for us. “Called client, no answer.” Be honest, most of us have written that.

The trouble is, six months from now nobody can tell when, which number, or what happened next. A note that vague is basically a sticky note in the rain.
case.ask: {name}, what's missing from “called client, no answer” that a supervisor would need six months from now?

task.say:
Okay, your turn to run the No Contact Protocol on John Doe's file. Start with Step 1, the internal review in the CMS Case Summary, and name the deadlines that are live right now. No dialling first.

Then rebuild the attempts already made, those two missing voicemails, and carry the Step 2 ladder forward in the Communications Log. Every attempt gets date, time, channel and outcome, plus the next action and its due date.

Then the fun part: a live call with Margaret Doe. {name}, you might be the one on the phone.

Say who you are, confirm she's the emergency contact on file, and ask her to have John call the firm by a set date. Confirm his best number and current address, all without sharing any case details.

That last part trips people up, because Margaret will ask, “Is he okay? Is the case okay?” Your answer is friendly and gives her nothing about the case.

Fair warning, emergency contacts aren't always thrilled to hear from us. I once had a mom pick up and say, “He's thirty-four, why am I still his answering service?”

You hand in a full Step 1 review, an unbroken Step 2 log, and your call on Step 3.

Keep this one: review first, dial second, log everything.
task.ask: {name}, before you log anything, which deadline is running on this file right now?

check.say:
Check your work against these, and let's talk about the difference between okay and excellent. Okay says, “I called, I emailed.”

Excellent shows Step 1 done first, with status, live deadlines and last contact reviewed. Both earlier voicemails are logged with date, time and channel.

The phone rung is cleared with at least two attempts, then email and text, not more calls. And Margaret is used, which is the rung people forget most.

Every entry has date, time, channel and outcome, plus a next action with a due date. Your Step 3 impact names the SOL of 02/06/2028 and the treatment that hasn't started. And nothing threatens to drop the case.

Here's why this matters down the road. That missing treatment start is the seed of the 14-Day Gap, a stretch with no doctor visits that an insurance company will use to cut the offer.

So here's your mystery, {name}. If John's silent now, what does the adjuster say about it in six months, and how does your log answer them?
check.ask: {name}, if you called his mobile three times, how many channels have you actually used?

case.say:
A note from Atty. Thorne just landed on the file, dated 02/21/2026. Before I read it, {name}, guess how many days it's been since we heard from John. Closer than you'd like?

Here it is. Eleven days, no word, and no treatment we know of.

The phone rung is cleared, emails and texts are out, Margaret Doe has been tried, and it's all logged.

Atty. Thorne wants the Final Warning Letter drafted for review Monday morning: every attempt with its date, a response date, and how to reach us, by certified mail and email.

Withdrawal is possible, not decided, and the letter says nothing about John's claim.

And here's the hard part. It has to be urgent but not threatening.

I've seen first drafts that read like a love letter, “please call when you get a chance, no rush,” and drafts that read like a ransom note. Neither one gets a call back.

The target: clear, dated, firm, and kind.
case.ask: {name}, give me one sentence that would make this letter sound threatening rather than urgent?

task.say:
You'll draft the Step 4 Final Warning Letter to John Doe in the Action Plan Editor, using the warning letter template.

List every earlier attempt with its date. Set a response deadline inside the 7 to 14 day window, warn that withdrawal is possible, and tell him exactly how to respond.

Every sentence stays inside the UPL line. UPL is the unauthorized practice of law, meaning giving legal advice when you're not a lawyer.

So nothing about how strong his claim is, nothing about what silence does to it legally, and nothing saying the case is being dropped.

Then write down what has to be true before a skip-trace can start, and whose approval Step 5 needs.

{name}, you'll read your opening line to the room when you're done, so make it a good one. You hand in a ready-to-send letter with both deliveries logged and the escalation recorded.

Remember: what we need and by when, never what happens to his case.
task.ask: {name}, whose approval does the Step 5 decision need, and where will you record that?

check.say:
Swap drafts with the person next to you and grade each other.

Fun fact: a good warning letter is the fastest way to make a missing client reappear. Half the time they call within the hour asking why we're being so dramatic.

First, {name}, read us the banned and compliant pairs out loud. It'll save someone a full rewrite.

Now, passable versus excellent. A passable letter says “as soon as possible.” An excellent one has a real date inside the 7 to 14 day window.

Look for the firm's name and file reference, and the date of loss, 02/06/2026. Earlier attempts listed with dates. Withdrawal reads as possible, not decided. At least two ways to respond.

Certified mail and email both recorded, address confirmed first. Nothing about claim value or legal consequence, so no “you will lose your case.” Skip-trace locks written down, Step 5 noted as Atty. Thorne's.

This one letter can be the difference between a client who comes back to finish treatment and a case that closes for nothing.

And your mystery: if John does call back, what's the very first thing you check on his file?
check.ask: {name}, does your partner's letter tell John what's needed and by when, without telling him what happens to his case?

questions.say:
Welcome to the game show portion of the day! Your answers come from this file, in your own words, typed under each question. But I'm going to warm you up out loud first.

{name}, lightning round: name the six steps of the No Contact Protocol, in order. Go. Anyone can steal if they stall.

On the test you'll set out all six steps with what's required at each. You'll also state the protocol's three purposes and say which one protects the firm rather than the client.

Here's a hint, because people answer this one shallowly. Protection from liability, meaning the firm can show it did its job if someone complains later, is the purpose most people leave out. And it's exactly why the record is built the way it is.

Then there's the case of the lazy colleague, who logged three voicemails on three days and called the ladder done. Tell me what's wrong, and what the log should show.

Remember: if it isn't logged with a date, it didn't happen.
questions.ask: {name}, which of the three purposes do you think is easiest to forget?

summary.say:
Now your Self-Summary, where you put the principles in your own words.

Here's the scenario. It's 04/08/2026. Riverton Spine & Rehab reports John Doe has missed two visits, he isn't answering anyone, and Dana Whitfield has asked John for a Recorded Statement.

Tell me what you do first, second and third, and what each step protects. {name}, I'll want to hear your first move out loud.

This one pulls it all together: the running SOL, a Treatment Gap that's hardening, and the claims work that has to keep moving anyway.

And keep in mind, the gap you're watching build here is the same 14 days defense counsel will ask John Doe about at his deposition on Day 5.

The habit to keep: for every step you take, know exactly what it protects.
summary.ask: {name}, of those three problems, which one protects the most if you deal with it first?

scale.say:
Last step is your Skill Scale. Rate yourself honestly, one to five, on each competency, then submit it.

One to five isn't a grade. It's just a snapshot of where you are today.

When I get these back, I'll compare your rating with your Knowledge Check score. Wherever there's a wide gap, either way, we'll have a short chat. Overrating and underrating both tell me something useful.

Fair warning: last batch, someone rated themselves a five on everything and then put Margaret Doe down as the defendant. We still talk about it.

Now, a mystery to take with you. John's transportation fell apart on 04/01, and his visits started slipping right after.

{name}, before tomorrow, dig through the file and tell me what we could've done the day his ride ended, like asking Riverton about transportation help, and who we should've told that same day.
scale.ask: {name}, which competency here are you least sure how to rate, and why?

why.say:
Game: what's the date? I give you a date, you tell me what's due. {name}, 04/07/2026. Anyone?

Here's a hint: count six weeks from John Doe's first therapy visit on 02/24/2026.

Got it? It was his week-6 mark of care, the day the doctors check whether therapy is actually working. And John Doe wasn't there.

map.say:
Here's the road for monitoring treatment before we dive in. Five steps, and {name}, I'm testing you on the middle three in about ninety seconds, so lock them in.

Then you run A-C-T. Assess, where medical danger goes to the provider and legal danger goes to Atty. Thorne. Coordinate, where you clarify with the office and remove the barrier.

And Track, where every fix attempt goes into a GIRP note, a short note of the Goal, the Intervention, the Response and the Plan. Facts only.

Okay, {name}, time's up. A, C, T. Go.

Check in, name it, run A-C-T. That's the whole loop.

theory.say:
Knowing the Standard Treatment Map is what separates a Case Manager who watches a recovery from one who drives it. Care that drifts off the map is what triggers denials and IMEs, the exams the insurance company orders from its own doctor.

Quick recap. Acute is days 1 to 14: the ER, imaging, first therapy and proving the crash caused the injury.

Sub-acute runs weeks 2 to 8: active therapy, specialists and measured gains. Restorative is weeks 9 to 24: injections, work hardening, which is therapy that rebuilds the strength for his actual job, and anything blocking a return to work.

Then maintenance: home exercise and visits as needed.

Maximum Medical Improvement, or MMI, is the doctor saying more care won't make him better. It closes treatment and opens the pre-demand.

When a client drifts off the map, you ask why first, before the funding stops. A watcher writes “missed visits.” A driver writes why, and what's being done about it. {name}, be a driver for me.
theory.ask: {name}, which phase do you think John Doe was in when he missed his week-6 mark?

theory2.say:
A few more ideas you'll lean on. The A-C-T protocol is your immediate move for any red flag: Assess the danger, Coordinate the fix and Track it. That record is what gives Atty. Thorne his why.

“Reasonable and necessary” is the insurer's test for paying. Is the care normal for this kind of crash, and is there a measurable gain, not just “I hurt less”?

SMART goals, meaning specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound, like the week-6 measures, are what hold up with doctors and adjusters alike.

And there's the stakeholder triad: the clinical loop, the legal loop and the money loop, with you as the switchboard in the middle. One broken loop can stall a case for months.

{name}, here's a fun one. “John will feel better soon” is a wish, not a goal. Turn it into a SMART goal for me.

The rule of thumb: if you can't measure it, it isn't a goal.
theory2.ask: {name}, what would a SMART goal for John Doe's next six weeks of therapy actually sound like?

frame.say:
Here's the map phase by phase, with a test at the end. {name}, keep your finger on John Doe's file.

Acute is days 1 to 14: the ER, an MRI or CT, a brace, rest and ice, and first therapy, while we establish causation, meaning the crash caused it, and PIP coverage.

Sub-acute is weeks 2 to 8, with active therapy two or three times a week and specialist follow-up. That's where the week-6 check lives, looking for 20 to 30 percent better range of motion.

Restorative is weeks 9 to 24: work hardening, injections, emotional adjustment and finding the barriers to going back to work.

Maintenance comes after week 24, with home exercise and visits as needed while we watch for the doctor's MMI finding. MMI is the finish line. Treatment closes, and the pre-demand audit opens.

And here's the money angle. An adjuster lays John's records over this exact map, and every spot where they don't line up is a spot where the offer drops.

Remember: off the map means off the money.
frame.ask: {name}, on 04/08/2026, day 61 of John Doe's file, where on this map is he sitting?

rules.say:
Now the rules. Monitor outcomes, not just attendance. Ask about visits, pain and what he can't do at work or home, and hunt the barriers: inside ones like fear or mood, outside ones like transport or money.

On 04/08/2026, day 61, he's in week 9. His week-6 mark fell on 04/07/2026, which is 02/24/2026 plus 42 days. The next step, whether that's medication, injections or a specialist, is the doctor's decision.

Name the variance before you fix it. Run A-C-T for every red flag, and adjust the plan first, because honestly, it's usually the plan, not the client.

Climb the ladder one documented rung at a time: clinical, then administrative, then legal. Write every intervention as a GIRP note.

You coordinate care; you never direct it. Never tell him to skip treatment, or that missed visits cut his claim.

And make friends with the clinic's front desk. The doctor runs the treatment, but the front desk runs the building, the schedule and possibly the weather. {name}, they'll know he missed before anyone.

One line to keep: you coordinate care, you never direct it.

Remember the order: PIP, then Peach State, then the LOP.

theory.say:
Four ideas, plain and simple, but a riddle first. One of these payers can pay a bill today and then come back after the settlement asking for its money back. {name}, tell me which one when we're done.

Once the claim's set up, the Case Plan runs on three pillars: clinical care, how he's functioning, and subrogation management, which is a fancy phrase for who gets paid back from the settlement.

The Payer Order is the default line: MedPay or PIP first, health insurance second, an LOP last. Keeping that order keeps the liens down.

PIP is coverage for Medical Bills regardless of fault, up to its limit. Health insurance pays covered care at its contract rate.

And a Letter of Protection is the client's signed agreement that a provider gets paid from any recovery. That makes it a lien on his net, meaning his take-home.

So, {name}, the riddle? It's the Health Plan. It can hold a reimbursement right against the recovery. Lovely people, Health Plans. They just like their money back.
theory.ask: {name}, which of these payers have you dealt with in your own life, and which one is first in line on John Doe's file?

theory2.say:
The other half is about keeping care moving. The Standard Treatment Map is the usual route: emergency, imaging, chiropractic and therapy, orthopedics, pain management, sometimes surgery. And every stop needs a payer.

Monitoring progress means checking real results, not ticking boxes. If you ask, “Hey John, how are you?” he says “Fine,” and you've learned nothing.

Try this instead: “How many visits did you make this week, what can you do now that you couldn't last month, and what might get in your way next week?”

Crisis intervention is stepping in when care gets denied or stuck in paperwork, and fixing the immediate problem first.

Pro tip: the fastest way to unstick a clinic is the one person in its billing office who actually answers the phone. They know which bill is stuck, why, and whose desk it's sitting on.

And watch for medication red flags, like an opioid, a muscle relaxant and a sedative together, or doses climbing with no new diagnosis. You don't judge that yourself. You raise it with the provider. {name}, you're up.

The takeaway: ask about results and barriers, never just “how are you.”
theory2.ask: {name}, instead of asking John Doe how he is, what's one question you'd ask him about his plan?

frame.say:
Here's the Payer Order, step by step, with a pop quiz hidden inside. {name}, one of these payers also covers lost wages. Shout it when you hear it.

First you identify the payers: every source and its default order. And remember, who's actually primary is Atty. Thorne's call, not ours.

Next is MedPay or PIP. Both pay regardless of fault, up to the limit. And there's your answer: PIP also pays 80% of lost income, where MedPay pays Medical Bills only.

Then comes the Health Plan, which pays covered care at its contract rate but may claim money back from the recovery.

The Letter of Protection is the last rung, for care the earlier payers can't carry, paid from any recovery on Atty. Thorne's terms.

Think of the ladder like this: every rung you skip on the way up is a rung John Doe pays for on the way out. {name}, climb it for me.
frame.ask: {name}, where is John Doe on this ladder for his Riverton Spine & Rehab physical therapy, and why?

rules.say:
Now the rules. In treatment, the question is always, “Is the plan working?” And you run the Payer Order: Harbor Point PIP, then Peach State, then an LOP.

John claims the $5,000 PIP as a passenger in Kevin Alvarez's 2020 Ford Escape, because no policy in his household carries PIP. PIP pays in date order, never wages.

When Crescent Pain & Spine billed Peach State on 05/15/2026 with $640.00 of PIP left, you tracked both ledgers and never re-routed a paid claim.

Riverton Spine & Rehab got an LOP because it's out of network. Summit Imaging's 03/11/2026 MRI went to PIP.

It's tempting to say yes to every LOP request, because it makes the provider go away. Don't. Prove from the ledger which payer should cover it.

LOP terms are Atty. Thorne's: you prepare, route, send once he approves, and confirm receipt.

I once had a billing manager call me four times in one morning about an invoice dated that same morning. She wanted it paid yesterday. {name}, you smile, log it, and never promise a provider an amount, a reduction or a date.

The line to keep: the ledger decides, not the loudest caller.
rules.ask: {name}, Riverton and Summit Imaging both asked for an LOP. Why did only one of them get it?

Picture a normal month on this file. A provider asks for an LOP.

You run the Payer Order and prepare one on counsel's template only for care PIP and Peach State can't carry, then route it for approval from CMS Documents, Outgoing. The payer check is recorded first, and nothing goes out without Atty. Thorne.

Clean numbers win arguments. Check every line against a visit.

dodont.say:
Time for 3 Clues, 1 Rule. I'll reveal three clues in turn. Call Do or Don't as soon as you've got it, and name the rule. {name}, you're scorekeeper.

Good habits include asking “Is the plan working?” at every contact, ending each call by asking what might get in the way of treatment this week, and fixing conflicting provider notes straight away.

Also telling John which payer handles which bill, because cost worry left unanswered is how a client stops going.

The traps: issuing an LOP just because a provider asked, telling a provider they'll be paid in full at settlement, mission creep, which means doing jobs that aren't yours, and handing Atty. Thorne raw records with no summary.

Now the mystery. In a few months, a statement is going to land asking John Doe to pay $1,540.00 on a bill his Health Plan already processed.

{name}, before the next lesson, think about it: does he owe it? The answer's hiding on a piece of paper that literally says THIS IS NOT A BILL.
dodont.ask: {name}, why is an LOP never really free for John Doe, even when the provider is happy with it?

why.say:
Show of hands: who's ever opened a letter from their health insurance, read the whole thing, and still had no idea whether they owed money? Keep it up if you just paid it to make it go away. Yeah. Me too.

That letter is called an EOB, an Explanation of Benefits, and it might be the most confusing document in America. It's not a bill. It's the Health Plan's report on what it did with a bill.

Today, you become the person who can actually read one.

Take out RS26, Peach State's EOB. {name}, find the bottom line: what does John Doe owe Crescent for the injection? The EOB says $0.00.

Every payer reports back. Peach State does it with an EOB, and Harbor Point does it with its PIP payment history.

Read line by line, they tell you what was billed, what was paid, what was written off and what John Doe may still owe.

Those papers are the proof behind every medical number in the demand and every lien we negotiate. Get them right, and nobody slips a wrong number past us.

Remember: an EOB is a report card, not a bill.
why.ask: {name}, reading RS26, what does John Doe actually owe Crescent Pain & Spine for the injection, and which line tells you?

theory.say:
Four terms, and one of them sounds like a robot from a space movie.

Every payer reports back on a bill: the Health Plan with an EOB, PIP with its payment history. And you read both before you ever touch a lien.

An EOB is the plan's account of one processed claim. Not a bill, just proof of who paid what.

Billed versus allowed is the first thing to see. Billed is what the provider charged. Allowed is what the plan agreed to pay under its contract. In network, the gap gets written off, which means it simply disappears.

Remark codes are the little codes that explain each line, and here's our robot: CO-45 is the write-off code. AC1 flags a possible accident.

And member responsibility, meaning the deductible, copay and coinsurance, is the most an in-network provider may bill the patient.

Skimming the total and moving on is how mistakes get through. Read every line, because every line is a number someone may try to put in front of John Doe later. {name}, quick one.

The key idea: billed is the wish, allowed is the reality.
theory.ask: {name}, which of these terms have you seen on your own Medical Bills, and what did it mean there?

theory2.say:
Four more ideas, and honestly, these are where money quietly gets lost.

Balance billing is when a provider bills the patient for the part the plan already wrote off. In network that isn't allowed, so it's an error. Not a lien, and not a debt.

The PIP payment history is the carrier's list of every check: the date of service, the amount paid and the limit remaining.

Exhaustion is what happens once that limit's spent. Later bills come back unpaid, and you send them to the next payer.

And reconciliation means matching every provider balance to each payer's EOB or check, so no bill that's already been paid ever becomes a lien against John Doe.

Here's a real one. A client once paid a balance bill because, and I quote, “it had a barcode, so it looked official.”

The barcode was very official. The bill was wrong. It took us two months to get his money back. {name}, help me out here.

Keep this one: a balance bill is an error to fix, never a debt to pay.
theory2.ask: {name}, if a provider bills John Doe for a write-off, is that a lien, a debt or an error?

frame.say:
Here's how you read an EOB, top to bottom, every single time. {name}, one of these steps is the one people skip, and it's the one that costs the client. Guess which as I go.

First, match the claim: the member ID, claim number, provider and date of service against the CMS treatment record.

Then go from billed to allowed: the charge, what the plan allowed, and the amount it wrote off.

Next is the patient's share, the deductible, copay and coinsurance, because member responsibility is the most a provider may bill.

After that, what the plan paid, with its date and its check or electronic payment number, since that's where any payback claim starts.

Read the remark codes. CO-45 explains the write-off, and AC1 flags an accident and the plan's right to be paid back.

Finally, reconcile and log it against the provider's statement and the lien register, and flag any balance billing.

So, the step people skip? That last one. They read it, nod, and never compare it to the provider's statement. That's how a $0.00 turns into a collections call.

Remember: you're not done reading until you've compared.
frame.ask: {name}, which step would you be most tempted to skip on a busy Friday, and why?

rules.say:
Here's the real one on John Doe's file. Peach State's EOB of 06/03/2026, claim PS-2605-449021, covers Crescent's 05/15/2026 epidural injection, a shot of medicine near the spine for pain. And it says THIS IS NOT A BILL.

Crescent billed $3,400.00 and the plan allowed $1,860.00. The $1,540.00 difference is Crescent's write-off. The plan paid $1,860.00, and member responsibility is $0.00.

CO-45 explains that write-off, and AC1 is how Peach State's right to be paid back attaches.

Now Crescent's 07/01/2026 statement asks John Doe for $1,540.00. That's a balance bill. Not a debt, not a lien.

You could forward it to John with “FYI.” Please don't. Document it, route it to Atty. Thorne that day, draft a correction request and tell John what's happening.

Peach State's claim starts at $1,860.00, never $3,400.00, and its accident questionnaire goes to Atty. Thorne. Harbor Point's five checks total $5,000.00, exhausted 06/26/2026.

You read and reconcile. {name}, whether he owes anything is counsel's call.

The takeaway: $0.00 member responsibility means $0.00, whatever the statement says.
rules.ask: {name}, Crescent's $1,540.00 statement: is it a lien we missed, or a bill nobody owes, and which EOB line proves it?

Two documents side by side, and a little detective work.

On the left is Peach State's EOB for claim PS-2605-449021, with that red stamp, THIS IS NOT A BILL. The line to keep: the EOB beats the statement, every time.

job.say:
Let's run it the way it happens on the file. An EOB arrives. You post billed, allowed, adjustment, paid and member share against the visit in CMS Liens and Documents, so the $1,860.00 plan payment is logged and claim PS-2605-449021 is linked to the visit.

A PIP check clears, and you post it on the PIP Log with the date of service and the limit remaining, until it ties to Harbor Point's history with $0.00 left after 06/26/2026.

Then a patient statement shows a balance. You compare it with the EOB's member responsibility, flag the $1,540.00, tell Atty. Thorne the same day and draft the correction request.

When Peach State's itemized lien arrives, you match each line to an EOB and to the collision, so only those lines stand.

And here's the payoff. At settlement, Peach State will want its money back. If you've matched every line, we pay back what's really owed.

If you haven't, they'll happily take more, and it comes straight out of John's check. {name}, think like a lien auditor for a second.

Every lien line needs an EOB behind it, or it doesn't stand.
job.ask: {name}, what would you do with a line on Peach State's lien that no EOB supports?

why.say:
Game time: Prove It. The adjuster says the gap proves John Doe healed. You've got thirty seconds to shout out everything you'd collect to prove he didn't. Go!

{name}, you're writing them up. Ooh, good list.

Now let's sort it into two boxes: things written down at the time, and things written up for the claim.

And here's the reveal on last block's mystery. The paper made before anyone thought about a claim is the 02/07/2026 Riverton Drug receipt, one day after the crash, for pain relief. Nobody wrote that for a lawsuit.

Records made at the time do the heavy lifting. Provider notes that place the pain at the collision, histories that agree, the EMS report and the work records, and later a causation opinion, which is a doctor's letter linking the injury to the crash.

Anything in the other box, a record made to order, destroys the very case it was meant to save.

The takeaway: made at the time beats made to order, every time.
why.ask: {name}, which item on our list would an adjuster find hardest to argue with, and why?

theory.say:
So here's what sits behind the paperwork. Continuity is proved by what the record already shows, never by what it's asked to say.

Continuity of care just means an unbroken path of treatment, each step following from the last. And that chain is exactly what an adjuster tests.

A Treatment Gap is any break in it, and adjusters read a gap as minor, healed or unrelated.

Records made at the time, written by EMS, doctors and employers as things happened, are your strongest proof, because nobody wrote them for the claim.

And consistent histories, the same story of how, when and where it hurts across every chart, make continuity believable.

On TV, the detective finds one magic clue. In real life, you find twelve boring receipts that agree with each other. Boring wins, every time.

{name}, before I ask, take a guess at who wrote the first thing about John Doe's neck.

Remember: the record proves continuity, not your explanation of it.
theory.ask: {name}, who on John Doe's file wrote something down about his neck before anyone thought about a claim?

theory2.say:
Four more ideas, and one of them can end a career.

A causation opinion is a treating doctor's opinion linking the injury to the collision. It's the bridge across a gap, and Atty. Thorne requests it, not us.

Record integrity means a record changes only by its author's own dated addendum, an added note with a date on it. Altering a record can be evidence tampering or fraud. That's the career-ender.

Excuse notes prove only what their author saw or ordered at a visit, so days nobody examined him need other proof.

And generic notes, ones that don't tie the complaints to the collision, weaken causation. Under A-C-T, those get flagged to Atty. Thorne. You don't fix them yourself.

It's so tempting to just call the clinic and ask them to “update” a note. Resist it. Flag it and let counsel decide.

{name}, now think about the week of 02/09.

The career-saving rule: you never ask anyone to change a record.
theory2.ask: {name}, what proves John Doe couldn't work 02/09 through 02/13, when no doctor saw him?

frame.say:
These are the treatment red flags, and each one is a gift to the defense. Before I go through them, {name}, guess which one shows up most. Hold it.

In physical therapy, more than 12 sessions with no gain and no specialist or imaging suggested reads as a stalled plan or over-treatment.

Passive care only, meaning heat packs, TENS, which is a little electrical pulse machine, and massage with no exercise, is feel-good care adjusters discount.

Two or more missed appointments let the defense say the injury wasn't serious. And surgery recommended before therapy or injections, outside an emergency, invites a challenge on whether it was reasonable and necessary.

In pain management, an opioid, a muscle relaxant and a sedative together, with doses rising, is a safety risk.

In the records, left and right switched, or notes about life stress instead of the crash, weaken both credibility and causation.

And the answer to my guess? Missed appointments, by a mile.

Takeaway: spot the red flag before the defense does, and raise it.
frame.ask: {name}, which of these red flags do you see on John Doe's file right now?

rules.say:
Okay, the rules. Continuity is proved by records made at the time, then by a doctor's opinion that reads them, and never by explanations made to order.

Read every history for three things. How it happened: the collision. When it started: 02/06/2026. Where it hurts: the neck and right arm, since the 2021 visits were low back.

If the therapy notes and Dr. Reyes disagree, flag it to Atty. Thorne that day. Never ask a provider to change, back-date or add to a record, and never order an excuse note.

why.say:
Quick game: guilty or not proven. I'll say a fact, and you tell me if it proves Keystone has to pay for John's neck.

Here's the twist: neither one is enough.

Proving negligence, that Smith was careless, is only half the battle in personal injury law. The other half is causation and damages.

That means proving this collision, and nothing else, caused his C5-C6 herniation, which is a disc bulging out between two neck bones, plus his Medical Bills and the right-arm symptoms he still has.

And Keystone already has two other causes lined up: the 14-day gap and his 2021 chiropractic visits.

The document that links the crash to the injury is the Causation Letter. On this file it's Dr. Alana Reyes's letter of 06/19/2026, and the demand, the rebuttal and every binder after it lean on it.

doc.say:
Before you ever handle one, let's open this document up. I'll save the punchline for last.

A Causation Letter is a formal opinion from a medical professional, a treating physician, a surgeon or an independent medical expert, linking the accident to the specific injuries.

Its legal purpose is the half negligence can't prove: that the defendant's conduct directly caused the harm, the medical expenses and the ongoing limitations claimed.

Its evidentiary role on our file, meaning the job it does as proof, is big. Dr. Reyes holds her opinions more likely than not, ties the herniation to 02/06/2026, and answers both the gap and the 2021 visits.

{name}, guess what your job with this letter is. Here's the punchline: you handle the letter's path, never its words.

Atty. Thorne requests it. You assemble the records and docket the follow-up, check it against the file when it lands, and file it and cite it.

And read it the same day. Don't just file it unread, because a wrong date in a doctor's letter is a gift to the defense.

Honestly, a Causation Letter that says “maybe” is a fortune cookie, not evidence.
doc.ask: {name}, which part of handling this letter belongs to you, and which part never does?

theory.say:
Four ideas sit under this lesson. First, the two halves. Duty and breach, meaning Smith had to drive safely and didn't, prove negligence. Causation and damages prove what it cost, and a claim needs both.

Second, who writes it: a treating physician or surgeon who examined the patient, or an independent medical expert who reviews the records. Dr. Reyes is John Doe's treating spine surgeon.

Third, reasonable medical probability, which simply means more likely than not. Words like “possibly” or “could be” generally fall short, and the exact standard is Atty. Thorne's to confirm.

A doctor writing “possibly” is basically a Magic 8-Ball answer: ask again later.

Fourth, prior conditions. A prior injury in the same body region turns the question into aggravation, meaning whether the crash made an old problem worse.

John Doe's 2021 care was for his low back, a different region, and Dr. Reyes says it's unrelated. {name}, which of those four would you bet the defense attacks first?

The phrase to remember: more likely than not.

You file it under Medical, dated 06/19/2026, and cite it on the Gap Explanation Record. And you never draft, edit or suggest a word of it.

{name}, I know the temptation: leave out the 2021 records so the doctor never sees them. Send them anyway.

A doctor who never saw the prior records gets taken apart at deposition, and her whole opinion goes down with her. Hiding records from your own expert is like hiding the map from your own driver.

The takeaway: give the doctor everything, write nothing for her.
